content: The inclusion of data related to withdrawal or re-challenge of treatment is permissible. However, it is critical to avoid overloading data collection systems with information that is not systematically utilized for patient care or program management. This is particularly important when electronic data systems are introduced, as there may be a tendency to collect excessive details. Such practices should be avoided as they waste resources and demotivate staff. In settings where the capacity for routine monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of minimum indicators is still developing, ministries of health and national programs may consider periodic analyses of medical records using simple sampling methodologies. These analyses can also include investigations into medication adherence and drug safety. For example, annual patient record reviews can be conducted efficiently by program staff with minimal financial and training resources, focusing on household contacts. In many contexts, service data for people living with HIV (PLHIV) on antiretroviral therapy (ART) are captured within electronic data systems. These systems enable various analyses using unique personal identifiers (UIDs) across different data systems, such as cohort analyses of PLHIV newly enrolled in HIV care who were screened for tuberculosis (TB), evaluated for TB preventive treatment (TPT) eligibility, started on TPT, and completed TPT. The use of UIDs facilitates the de-duplication of entries and enhances data reliability for program management. Monitoring TPT completion is essential for both individual patient care and program management. Electronic data capture tools should record treatment outcomes for each individual starting TPT. The minimum number of doses required to determine completion for different regimens is outlined in relevant guidelines. Additional outcomes related to TPT adherence are proposed to aid in decision-making for patient care. National TB and HIV programs utilize various tools, such as patient cards, medical histories, case files, or electronic medical records, to document TPT services. A significant challenge in scaling up TPT services is the need to capture diverse data, often relying on paper-based records and the involvement of multiple healthcare providers. Programs monitoring preventive TB treatment (PMTPT) frequently use paper tools, such as household contact investigation lists or additional columns in ART registers, to record TPT initiation among PLHIV. These tools are periodically reviewed to derive indicators, often requiring manual computation. The printing and updating of paper records add to the workload of healthcare workers. Data from TB programs are increasingly being recorded electronically for individuals with TB disease requiring treatment, including ART. These databases are used to generate M&E indicators and track patient treatment responses. However, for PMTPT activities, many programs have yet to establish systematic electronic data collection mechanisms to generate programmatic indicators. The World Health Organization (WHO) advocates for the development of existing or new electronic systems to capture data elements necessary for PMTPT care and monitoring, enabling the automatic generation of indicators. If routine programmatic monitoring of TPT is still being established, an annual review of medical records can be conducted to evaluate key indicators, such as the proportion of household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients investigated for TB, those eligible for TPT who were prescribed treatment, those who initiated TPT, and those who completed TPT. The number of household contacts investigated, those who started TPT, and those who completed TPT should be documented on the respective index patient’s card. Only household contacts living in the same residence as the index patient should be recorded. The review process involves several steps: randomly sampling at least 12 health facilities treating TB patients, retrieving medical records of index patients from the same quarter of the previous year, counting and categorizing household contacts, and communicating the totals to the national team. The national team compiles the data and calculates the proportions for the indicators. This sampling method ensures national representativeness and does not require sophisticated statistical analysis. Missing data should be recorded and reported, and corrective actions should be taken if the proportion of missing data exceeds 30%. The WHO has developed a mobile application to support PMTPT monitoring and evaluation. This app allows healthcare workers to collect person-specific data and visualize it on an online dashboard for real-time monitoring. It can be adapted to meet country-specific program needs and has been field-tested in high-burden countries. The app’s second generation includes user-friendly features and improved integration with other information systems. Full implementation requires local software development, data hosting decisions, and staff capacity building. As the number of individuals evaluated for TPT increases, along with the diversity of TPT regimens and the need for disaggregated data by subpopulations, investment in electronic recording systems becomes increasingly important. These systems enable accurate quantification, procurement, and supply of consumables and support human and financial resource planning. With greater access to affordable hardware, software, and connectivity, real-time monitoring of PMTPT performance becomes more feasible. Dedicated M&E staff should be trained and assigned to coordinate and build capacity at national and subnational levels for data-driven decision-making. Countries should allocate budgets for digitizing data capture and reporting and seek donor funding if necessary. Providing optimal TPT and care involves the disclosure of personal information to the healthcare system, which must be handled with the utmost confidentiality. Sensitive information should only be shared with individuals directly involved in care and securely stored. Paper-based records should be minimized and destroyed when no longer needed. Computerized databases containing sensitive information should be protected with passwords and encryption, with access rights granted based on user roles. Assigning UIDs to individuals evaluated for or receiving TPT can aid in matching and de-duplication of entries. Personal details should be removed as soon as they are no longer required for reporting purposes. Programs should develop policies to ensure the confidentiality of personal data, aligned with national policies where applicable. Information on data handling should be included in counseling for individuals offered TPT. Just as individuals have the right to opt out of TPT, their decisions regarding the use of their personal information should also be respected. Supportive supervision is a critical component of routine M&E for health facilities. It includes quality checks for data recording and reporting, validation of case files, and completeness of data collection tools. National programs may provide standard checklists to assess data quality and implementation across the care cascade. Supervisory visits may also gather data for health management information system (HMIS) reporting. At least once a year, a data quality audit of routine monitoring systems should be conducted, involving members of TB and HIV programs and other relevant stakeholders. Ethical considerations in TPT implementation emphasize the importance of informed decision-making. Only 5–10% of individuals infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis will develop TB disease in their lifetime, with higher risks for certain groups such as PLHIV, young children, and those recently infected. TPT should be administered after evaluating the benefits versus potential harms. Routine testing and treatment should be limited to groups with demonstrated risk of progression to TB disease. TPT must always be an individual choice, made with full information and without coercion. Counseling services should be strengthened to ensure effective communication about the benefits, risks, and uncertainties of TPT. Proactive measures, including routine clinical and laboratory monitoring, should be integral to PMTPT to ensure patient safety. Informed consent is generally required for TPT, as the subject does not pose an immediate risk to others, and the potential benefits are context-specific. Effective communication of uncertainties, risks, and benefits is essential. Nurses and frontline healthcare workers can be trained to counsel individuals about TPT, interpret test results, and discuss the implications of TPT on families and communities. National programs should develop culturally and linguistically appropriate communication strategies to convey the benefits, risks, and uncertainties of TPT. Feedback should be regularly invited to adjust program implementation, and counseling efforts and informed consent should be systematically documented and monitored.
